utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could I have the appearances, Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Dermot Groome and also representing the Prosecution here today is Doris Brehmeier-Metz, Amir Zec and we are assisted by Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. And for the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Geert-Jan Knoops, myself, and assisted by co-counsel Mr. Wayne Jordash and legal assistants, Ms. Anne-Marie Verwiel, Ms. Amy Walsh and Ms. Rima Dykstra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. The Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Zoran Jovanovic, attorney, and today, together with Vladimir Domazet and Mrs. Ingrid Morgan, we represent the accused Franko Simatovic as Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. Could we just verify, Mr. Simatovic, that you can hear me in a language you understand? The microphone --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. THE ACCUSED SIMATOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simatovic. On our agenda today is the opening statement to be delivered by the Prosecution. Before we can move to that, we first have to pay attention to the fact that Mr. Stanisic is not present in court. Mr. Knoops, we have received a form in which we find a report from the UNDU about the non-attendance in court. There is also a form, absence from court due to illness, in which it appears that Mr. Stanisic says that he's unable to attend court proceedings on this date due to illness, that he has discussed the matter with counsel, and that he has not waived his right to be present. Now we had some confusion last time, but this time the empty box remains empty, from what I understand. Then we have received the observations by the principal officer and the UNDU medical service, and finally we have received a report by Dr. Eekhof, reporting medical officer. These documents have been filed this morning. We find on these forms, Mr. Knoops, apart from the expression of Mr. Stanisic that he feels not well enough to attend court, also that he does not want to follow the proceedings through a videolink. Are you informed about the reasons why Mr. Stanisic doesn't want to go to the videolink room and follow the proceedings from there? Is there anything with the technicalities of that or does he have any difficulties in moving to that place? Could you inform us about the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would -- later on would like to submit a formal application to the Court, but now that the Court has invited the Defence to comment on this aspect, we can inform the Court that both Mr. Jordash and I went to see the defendant this morning, just before the medical examination, and we were informed that Mr. Stanisic is not able to participate at this videolink conference purely based on his mental condition. So it has nothing to do with the technicalities, but purely on the basis of his mental stage at this moment. And to this extent, we have just filed courtesy copies to the Prosecution of the report of Dr. Petrovic of the 10th of May, which was referred to in the first report of Dr. Eekhof of 11th of May; and if the Legal Officer is so kind to distribute the copies to the Justices. We find support in this report for this conclusion that Mr. Stanisic is not able to participate -- apart from physical aspects is not able to participate on the basis of his mental condition. And we believe that this support is also re-affirmed by the reports today filed by Dr. Eekhof and the accompanying report of the -- I believe the medical service, column 4(A). So in sum, it's the position of the Defence that Mr. Stanisic is mentally not able to participate during any alternative, namely, the videolink conference apart from the fact that he is not able to be transported at all to the court according to the report of Dr. Eekhof. If Your Honours wish me to continue, we can also wait for the moment to submit a formal application to the Court after potentially hearing Dr. Eekhof on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, we will have an opportunity to put further questions to Dr. Eekhof, but Dr. Eekhof comes to a different conclusion, that Mr. Stanisic is fit enough to participate in proceedings from -- through a videolink. Because you referred to apparently someone who says, on the one hand, I confirm that he has no observable symptoms with which I can judge whether or not he's too unwell to attend court and at the same time gives an expectation that it will be different than one day. It's not easy to understand how you could establish one and conclude the other. But reference is made to the report of the reporting medical officer, who confirms that there's still a depression. So therefore, I think we should first of all consider whether we have any additional questions to be put to Dr. Eekhof. Then after that you can make your submission. And finally then the Chamber will decide whether and how to proceed. In order to put any further questions to Dr. Eekhof, I'd like to establish the videolink with the UN Detention Unit. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, I can see you at this moment. Can you see me?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I cannot hear you yet but it might be that I have to move --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, I think I forgot to push on the mute button, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now can hear you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I can hear you very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We received a report dated the 9th of June in -- and I just briefly read the conclusions. You come to the conclusion that Mr. Stanisic is not fit to be transported, that he's not fit to sit for more than ten minutes, that he is fit enough to participate in proceedings if sitting is limited to ten minutes, and that he's fit enough to participate in proceedings up to one hour in the bed that has been installed in the video teleconference room. I would like to give an opportunity to the parties to ask for additional information, and it may well be that we then would still have some additional questions for you as well. Mr. Groome, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a couple of brief questions. Good afternoon, Dr. Eekhof. The first question that I would like to ask you is in paragraph 5 of the report you drafted today, the 9th of June, you say that: "He," meaning Mr. Stanisic, "declined the offer by Dr. Falke to consult a psychiatrist." Do I take it from that that Mr. Stanisic was offered an opportunity to meet with someone who could discuss his mental state but that he declined such an offer?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is true. He declined it for the reason that he wasn't prepared to tell all his story and all his problems to a new psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've heard Mr. Knoops say that the sole reason for Mr. Stanisic not being here today is because of his mental state, as he perceives it himself. Having heard that, does that change your opinion with respect to your first conclusion, he is not fit to be transported?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] He is not fit to be transported on somatic grounds not on psychiatric --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But now having heard Mr. Knoops say that Mr. Stanisic is not putting forward any somatic grounds for his inability to be present here, does that change your opinion as to whether he could be transported here if he chose to come to court?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, as he still has his somatic problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: By the way, this was only mentioned in reference to the videolink conference. Prosecution was summarising the Defence comments, I think, in a different context. Dr. Eekhof, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good afternoon, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: As you may remember, last week we were questioning you on the same subject, namely, the underlying basis of your own observation that there are, in your view, no evident psychiatric reasons preventing him from participating in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Was -- after Tuesday, was there a new psychiatric evaluation conducted by Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have difficulties in hearing you, Dr. Eekhof. Is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I get a bit nearer to the microphone. Can you hear me better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So, Dr. Eekhof, that means that the foundation of the report also of 9th of June is relying on the report of Dr. Petrovic of the 10th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, yes, and my own observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, the Defence was able to retrieve a copy of the report of Dr. Petrovic of the 10th of May, which is now in possession of the Justices and the Prosecution, and in the second paragraph of this report, in line 9, it's said: "His intellectual efficiency is fluctuating, same as his overall participation." Are you familiar with this comment of Dr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Not completely. When I talked with him he's able to discuss his illness. Of course I do not discuss the case, but his state of his illness and his complaints were -- he's very well able to discuss it. But as I stated in my report, I'm not a psychiatrist. But as far as I can see it, as a general practitioner who has training in psychiatry, I think that he's able to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But in your previous report you state every time that the psychological condition's unchanged, and during that you refer to the report of Dr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So actually, now that Dr. Petrovic is saying that his intellectual efficiency to participate is fluctuating, same as his overall participation, isn't it so that this isn't changed at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Sorry, I do not understand your question. What has not changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: His intellectual efficiency is fluctuating as same -- the same as his overall participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It is -- in the meetings I have had with Mr. Stanisic, it was not a question I had. Of course his state of mind is fluctuating, but there is a difference between being depressed as a state of mind and depression as an illness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And Dr. Petrovic also writes in the first paragraph that his depressiveness and apathy has become permanent.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is not completely my observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But you do refer to her report, and in the subsequent reports you say that his psychological state has been unchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you agree with me that the report of Dr. Petrovic is at this moment the only foundation to have any grasp as to his psychological situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, it is -- as a GP, I have to base my opinion on reports of specialists but also on my own observations and on diagnoses which I make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, today, for the first time in your reporting system you say that in your opinion a report by Dr. De Man on the present psychological and psychiatric state would provide us with an expert view and advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: What is the reason that you make this suggestion now?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] In fact, the suggestion -- I talked about De Man last time in the report. I mentioned Dr. De Man on the last report -- on the previous report, I'm sorry. And at this moment as there's a difference in opinion, partly between Mr. Stanisic and me, and, as you said, Dr. Petrovic, over his state of mind, that's why I suggested it would be a good idea to have an expert give his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So this is also based on your -- on the fact that you're not entirely sure whether there is indeed any psychiatric reason preventing him from participating in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It's to exclude that there would be psychiatric reason included in the proceedings. It is normal -- even if we know the diagnosis, even if we are quite sure in our profession to seek advice from specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: All right. The observation that Mr. Stanisic is fit enough to participate in the proceedings up to one hour in the bed that has been installed in the VTC room, is it correct that the term "fit" in this context is used in the context of somatic reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Somatic and psychological reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Now you just said that -- to exclude any possibility that Mr. Stanisic is not able to participate in the proceedings on mental reasons. Is it your opinion that any further proceedings should be based on such a report?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] If the report is made as suggested, then that would be a base to continue or to install treatment or to change the treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Now, has there been any psychotherapeutic treatment of Mr. Stanisic since the 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It has been offered but he has refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, you just said that Dr. Falke offered to consult psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, for him to consult, offered him a consultation with a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, I'm speaking about a treatment -- was there any treatment --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] -- with a treating psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But Dr. Petrovic left, I believe, shortly after Mr. Stanisic arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's correct, and she will not be back until the end of the month, that's why Dr. Falke offered to consult for treatment as a treating doctor another psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And when was this offer made?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Last week. So we can conclude that since the departure of Dr. Petrovic until this offer there was no treatment of Mr. Stanisic in a psychotherapeutic sense; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And do you agree with the view that Dr. De Man, being aware of the background and history of the case, would be the best suitable person to consult or to ask to file a report?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I think he would be the best man to file a report and to give advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And can you understand the reason why Dr. -- why Mr. Stanisic is in this stage, from his perspective, is preferring somebody who knows his story already instead of having a new psychiatric evaluation by a new specialist? Can you understand that reason?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] What I was saying we offered -- he was offered a treating psychiatrist, not an evaluation, last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Eekhof, this morning we were informed that the medication changed of Mr. Stanisic; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct. That is regarding his colitis. He was [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Because we read in your report of the 9th of June that the colitis showed some signs of inflammation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes. We monitored him so closely that at the least sign of change, we -- Dr. Falke consulted Dr. Cazemir, and together they decided to change the medication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So based on this inflammation, is it fair to say that his somatic situation also decreased -- increased, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, his well-being has not changed much. The general condition hasn't changed much. What we are doing now is reacting on the earlier signs of any common complications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We were informed that Mr. Stanisic is now being given the medication Tramadol; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is that akin to some kind of a morphine?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, it's not an opiate. It's related but it is not under the group of opiate and does not have the same effects on the mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, we were informed that this medication does affect the state of mind, the level of concentration, and the ability to use intellectual capacities. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Why, it is possible that it does like a lot of other medication, but not the way an opiate would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So it cannot be excluded that the change of medication and the effects of this medication could be of influence on his mental state of mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, it cannot be excluded completely, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We were also informed that the bleeding of Mr. Stanisic restarted which was evidenced by the samples of his urine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, Mr. Stanisic -- no, the -- we are talking about two different bleedings. The bleeding in his urine is continuous. We only monitor the quantity of it. And the other bleeding he's talked about is from colitis, which was reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: My last question, Dr. Eekhof, is: The formular which is attached to your report which is titled "UNDU Medical Service, Questions 1, 2, 4, and 5," it was answered in regards to column 4(A): "Including today, I assessed that he will require a one-day absence before he should be fit to attend court once more." Have you noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Was this approved by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It was approved by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So actually you're saying that for today Mr. Stanisic is not fit to attend court?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's the benefit of the doubt which we have as treating doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Right. But the term "fit," is this mentioned here or used here in a somatic mental or somatic and/or mental sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Fitness in the medical world is also somatic and mental.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you are actually that also mentally, for today Mr. Stanisic cannot attend court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, in total -- the total is not able to be in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your final --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Until he's been seen by Dr. Falke. That's [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And does this also include the videolink conference for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And your ultimate advice to the parties in this courtroom today is that preferably a further psychiatric evaluation by Dr. De Man should be conducted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops. Mr. Knoops --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof does not have to give any advice to the parties in this court. He can give his opinion. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I look to my -- no questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. It was not that Dr. Eekhof could not give advice, but you asked him to advise all the parties in this court and that's of course for the Chamber to decide. So any advice should be addressed to the Chamber or to no one else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Eekhof, I have a few questions for you. You said that you considered that Mr. Stanisic was not able to attend court that, I would say, already follows from your observation that he's not fit to be transported. I might have questions on that at a later stage, but then Mr. Knoops asked you whether that would also be true for attending court through the videolink. And I think you answered in the affirmative. Now, in your report of this morning I read that Mr. Stanisic is fit enough to participate in proceedings up to one hour in bed in the VTC room. I have some difficulties in reconciling what you just said and what I find in the report of -- that was given this morning. Could you help me out?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, when I visited Mr. Stanisic I made my own conclusion. I observed him. I talked with him. And my report is based on that fact. As a doctor, say somebody reports ill, a further assessment is necessary, and I told Mr. Knoops that until then, as a treating doctor, the patient has the benefit of the doubt. I do not have new information which would change my initial report. That's what I said. Maybe not a real legal answer, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, apart from a legal answer I do not fully understand the answer. That's my problem. This morning you said he's able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- follow the proceedings through a videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, and he reported ill after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He reported ill after that, and you say because he reported ill, I have to give him the benefit of the doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, based on my report he is fit to sit in the video teleconference room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you establish any change since you have written this report this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore the conclusion would be the same, although in view of the fact that Mr. Stanisic feels he is too ill, that you should give him the benefit of the doubt for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The only change in opinion would be the benefit of the doubt at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you said he is not fit to be transported. Is that for the reasons of physical illness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] For physical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would that be the herniated disc which causes the problem and together with the colitis?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] At this moment, the colitis is a big problem. I'd like to point out he does -- he has lower-back pain, but it's not based on herniation at this moment; that has been excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And no other cause has been established at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to me why it was -- how I have to understand that it was possible to transport Mr. Stanisic from Belgrade to The Hague, where apparently transportation is not in any way possible between the UNDU and the Tribunal's premises where we are at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The back pain got much worse after his -- on his arrival here. I did not examine him beforehand, but that is the reason at this moment. That's also the reason why we are planning a rehabilitation programme with a physiotherapist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you earlier reported that he had refused physiotherapeutical treatment. No start has yet been made. Has he approved already to be treated by a physiotherapist?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I just got the report in, so I do not know if he has agreed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So matter is as it was before, that he had not given his consent up to this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you did not examine Mr. Stanisic before he left Belgrade. What's, then, the exact basis for the observation that the back pain has become far worse?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, I did -- I was present on his arrival at Schiphol and the way he walked out of the plane with some difficulties, but not the difficulties he's showing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at present, walking, moving around, is that -- can he get out of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It's still very limited. As far as we can see, it's getting a little bit more often, but still very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could he -- that we do not find that in the report. Could he, for example, walk to the videolink room?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] No, he claims not to be able to. I cannot check it, but I assume he's not able to walk to the videoconference room --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] It would be about 20, 30 metres to the lift and then about 10 metres here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it's your observation that you think he would not be able to go there. As the parties are aware, the Chamber has, I think, informed the parties that the Chamber would seek additional information when needed. From the information we received - and that's now put on the record - it was observed that Mr. Stanisic can move to a cell for smoking. Could you explain to us why you consider him not to be able to go to the videolink cell, whereas he is apparently able to go to the smoking cell and stay there for a while to smoke?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Well, that -- in fact, it is not, from my point of view, important if he can walk it or not, as he's been provided a wheelchair, so he can be brought to the videoconference room without any problems. So his walking capacity is not a factor in being able to be present in the video teleconference room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may be true. It's not an answer to my question. Is he moving to the smoking cell while using a --

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not aware of that. Has it been considered for transportation purposes to -- to find solutions, for example, transport in a more horizontal position rather than normally be seated on a chair in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm not aware of a -- that question has never been put to me, so I cannot answer it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore your conclusion that he's not fit to be transported is -- could also depend on the conditions of transportation; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. A final question to you, you said he would be able to participate in proceedings up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time of rest would you consider appropriate before resuming? Would that be half an hour? 40 minutes? 20 minutes? One hour? Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] This is always a very difficult -- it's always more or less a guess. I think after a recovery period of one hour he could proceed further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answers. I've no further questions for you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be possible for me to ask a follow-up question for a matter that arose during Your Honour's questioning of Dr. Eekhof?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, when Judge Orie was asking you some questions about Mr. Stanisic, you were describing what you are characterizing as increased lower-back pain. Now, looking at a report that was filed on the 15th of May, it seems that there -- an MRI did not reveal any underlying organic reason for the back pain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So am I correct in saying that your characterisation of the level of back pain is based upon Mr. Stanisic's own reports that the back pain is becoming worse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] In the case of lower-back pain without herniations, we -- it's the only thing we can rely on as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the parties. I don't think that we need the further presence and assistance of Dr. Eekhof. That being confirmed, Dr. Eekhof, I would like to thank you very much for making yourself available and we'll close the videolink. At least I can't see you anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. EEKHOF
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knoops, you announced that you'd make an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Jordash will file the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, could you give us any impression on how much time you would you need for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The application is for an adjournment of today's hearing and tomorrow's hearing in order to have Mr. Stanisic seen and diagnosed by Dr. De Man. We rely upon both Dr. Eekhof, who, as Your Honours know, recommends that such a diagnosis should take place, and we rely upon the report from Dr. Petrovic which buttresses that suggestion. The report is dated the 10th of May, 2009, and, as Your Honours know, indicates that his -- Mr. Stanisic's overall psychological functioning has worsened. And so we submit the same benefit of the doubt that Mr. -- Dr. Eekhof gave to the accused exists and will continue to exist until a psychiatrist, and preferably Dr. De Man because he's the one who has the history and a clearer picture of Mr. Stanisic over a long period of time. Before he has seen him, the Court, in our submission, will be returned again and again to this same debate, which is Dr. Eekhof, as a general practitioner, coming to conclusions which are undoubtedly well thought out from his perspective, but coming to conclusions which he himself caveats constantly with, "We ought to have the benefit of a specialist." "I might be wrong" is the subtext to his detailed but caveated opinion. And in our submission, this situation to a large degree has existed for some time. We had a report from Dr. De Man dated the 19th of March, which led to the Prosecution's application to re-call Mr. Stanisic for further treatment in -- sorry, for diagnosis at the Pieter Baan Centre in Amsterdam. We -- or Your Honours returned Mr. Stanisic to detention. And since that time Mr. Stanisic has only seen Dr. Petrovic. That is the only psychiatric diagnosis which he has had since that time. And there is no evidence on the record from a psychiatrist since Mr. Stanisic's re-call which has indicated anything other than there is a serious problem. And we accept, of course, that Mr. Stanisic declined the offer, but we would submit that a reasonable position to take in relation to someone who is ill, whether that is a minor physical illness which has been ongoing for some time or whether, in the case of Mr. Stanisic, it is a serious and long-standing psychiatric condition, it makes sense, we submit, for Mr. Stanisic to see a psychiatrist who is fully cognizant of the history; and it makes sense, we submit, and it's realistic for Mr. Stanisic to say, Well, I'd rather not describe the inner recesses of my mind and my depression to a new person. And so we submit every single pointer is suggesting more information is needed before Your Honours could rule that the trial at this stage should proceed. We are not asking for an adjournment of several months; simply, these two afternoons so that Dr. De Man can visit, diagnose, and then when we return to court we're all, and particularly Your Honours, in a better position to decide what to do and to decide if those veiled suggestions concerning Mr. Stanisic's reluctance to come to court are in fact justified, or in fact the diagnosis supports his position that he's not well enough to come to court or attend the video conferencing room. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Groome, do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With respect to Mr. Jordash's submissions, a couple of observations. Once again, I think we're running into a problem that's -- that arose last year and I think it's starting to make itself quite apparent here is this conflation of the assessing of Mr. Stanisic and the treatment of Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Stanisic and Dr. De Man have -- they've never had a therapeutic relationship. Dr. De Man was a Court-appointed expert asked to give his professional opinion about Mr. Stanisic. It may be true that Mr. Stanisic needs some psychiatric treatment and it may be true that if Dr. Petrovic can only see him what seems to be at intervals of six weeks, that he may need more than that. And certainly if it's the assessment of Dr. Falke and Dr. Eekhof that he would benefit from more regular and predictable psychiatric therapy, the Prosecution certainly would have no opposition to that. But it's clear that Dr. De Man is not the person to be doing that if he is to maintain his position as a Court-appointed expert to give his professional opinion and his assessment about Mr. Stanisic to Your Honours. I must take issue with what Mr. Jordash is putting forward now as -- he's jumping or asking the Chamber to draw the conclusion that Dr. Eekhof's suggestion, that it may be a good idea to ask Dr. De Man to look at Mr. Stanisic, as undermining his own conclusion. And I would draw the Chamber's attention to page 9 of today's transcript beginning at line 19 where when Mr. Knoops put this proposition to Dr. Eekhof, he said: "It is normal even if we know the diagnosis, even if we are quite sure in our profession to seek the advice from specialists." I submit that Dr. Eekhof's suggestion that it might be beneficial to have Dr. De Man's view on it is not him expressing any doubt in his own opinion which we have in his report dated from today in which he says: "There are no evident psychiatric reasons preventing him from participating in proceedings." It is simply a statement of Dr. Eekhof of what any careful and prudent physician would say when an expert might be invited to participate in an assessment. I believe that there is a sufficient basis, Your Honour, on the -- all of the evidence that's before you to suggest that Mr. Stanisic can participate in proceedings today and that -- the Prosecution submits we should move forward. I'd also ask before I sit down for the Chamber to consider -- it seems clear that Mr. Stanisic could be brought in a wheelchair to the video conference link to -- if the Chamber has any doubt about this, to give some consideration to whether it might not be prudent to have Mr. Stanisic brought so the Chamber can make its own assessment of his state of mind and his ability to participate. And finally, Your Honour, I would just say that what we're -- what was on the agenda today is the opening of the Prosecution and that is somewhat different from every other aspect of the trial, and that is really the one part of the trial where there is no active participation by an accused. The opening that I am going to give today is in substantial part similar to the one I gave a year ago, that Mr. Stanisic has had over a year to discuss it with his attorney. It is quite possible for the Chamber or I would even request that the Chamber consider issuing an order requiring a video copy of the opening be provided to Mr. Stanisic within 48 hours of the opening so he could again sit down with Mr. Knoops and Mr. Jordash and fully discuss this. And also the opening is a mere expounding on the pre-trial brief which Mr. Stanisic has had in his possession for approximately two years. So there really is no active role for Mr. Stanisic to play. As far as the content of the opening, that could be given to him fully by this evening or tomorrow. So I submit, Your Honour, that there really is no basis for us not proceeding today with the Prosecution opening. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I briefly respond, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend makes several suggestions, noting that Dr. Eekhof is merely being prudent and that Your Honours might equally be prudent by having the accused brought to court in a wheelchair. So we're really not arguing about much. We both agree that it would be prudent to obtain further information about Mr. Stanisic's condition. Now, in our submission, before we start to bring somebody who potentially may be seriously psychiatrically ill to court in a wheelchair, we ought to take the suggestion which has been made by the doctor, Dr. Eekhof, which is the prudent suggestion that we have a psychiatric assessment and sooner rather than later. And prudence is the right way because we are talking about a major war crimes case about to start and prudence suggests that we should be sure if there is a viable and relatively straightforward way of satisfying ourselves or the Court's minds as to Mr. Stanisic's illness. And my learned friend makes the further suggestion that, well, it's the opening statement and therefore not much will happen and we can give the opening statement to the accused tomorrow. But we're back to the same place. If it's prudent to require further diagnosis, prudent for Your Honours to see the accused, it's prudent to assume that whatever mental condition Mr. Stanisic might be suffering will not entirely allow him to read the opening tomorrow. So it matters not whether we take the opening in a bundle of paper or we try to have Mr. Stanisic listen to it on a video conferencing system. If he's ill, he's ill, and we won't know that until we take, in our submission, this next step. Those are our submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add. The Prosecution, as you may recall, last Tuesday I was standing here. I made the suggestion to the Court, I said, We are back in the same position as last year if we don't learn a lesson from the past, i.e., that we re-call a psychiatrist for evaluation. I recall that Mr. Groome was supporting my submission. Your Honours can remember that. Mr. Groome was supporting my submission that we should have a psychiatric evaluation before the start of the case. Now today the Prosecution apparently changed their mind, but we as Defence, we have alerted the Chamber to the situation that it is absolutely, also from the perspective of efficiency of this case, worthwhile to have this evaluation in place before the start of the case. And I think it's important to notify the Court that the same Prosecution today apparently changed their mind while Dr. Eekhof's report is actually more in support of our submissions than last week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just wouldn't want my silence to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be misunderstood --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- to be misinterpreted as -- misunderstood as consent. The point I simply made last week, and I think I discussed with the Chamber and the Chamber responded, is just the Prosecution continues to view it as essential that the treatment and the assessment be separated. So I don't oppose whatever assessments are done. That's not the same as saying that I believe that we need to stop proceedings for that assessment process. I was simply saying to the Chamber I thought that it was imperative that, as soon as possible, we have a completely independent assessment procedure established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for -- I think in Latin one says if it's for a longer period of time sine die, but I would say sine hora which means the time the Chamber will need to decide whether the application should be granted or not. We do not know yet, but let's say that we'll certainly not resume before 20 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I deliver the ruling of the Chamber on the matters we discussed before the break, I first inform the parties that a decision was filed today to include in the modalities for trial, to that extent it's an amendment to the modalities of trial, to include regular reporting by an independent psychiatrist every two months. The Chamber has carefully considered all the submissions made by the parties and reject the request for an adjournment. This decision will be given in writing with all the reasons, but just to give a very summary explanation and the language not being authoritative, the Chamber finds that no objective medical reasons were established that would disable the accused to follow the proceedings, if not in court itself at least through a videolink. Again, the reasons will be set out in a written decision that will follow soon. The application by the Defence was to adjourn the proceedings and to order an examination, a psychiatric examination, so as to exclude for the possibility that psychiatric reasons could oppose against a continuation of the proceedings. That of course is implicitly rejected as well but will be dealt with also in the written decision. And as a result of the decision filed today, which you may not have seen yet but you will understand that it was not drafted the last 15 minutes, we discussed the matter earlier, that we were -- the Chamber expects to receive relatively soon a new psychiatric report. The Chamber has considered how to proceed and the Chamber would like the Registrar to send a copy of the following lines to the United Nations Detention Unit so that Mr. Stanisic will be informed about the decision by the Chamber, the decision that a request for adjournment has been rejected due to the fact that no objective medical reasons were established that would disable the accused to follow the proceedings, if not in this courtroom then through a videolink, which would also allow for the accused to further consider whether he wants to follow the proceedings from the video room. For that purpose we will again adjourn and the Chamber would like to be informed about once this message has been conveyed to the accused whether he wants to follow the proceedings through the videolink, and as the parties may understand, it will have some consequences for how long sessions would be, how long breaks would be. Therefore, the Chamber would like to be informed, if possible within 15 minutes, about the result of this information to be conveyed to the accused. We will resume at a quarter past 4.00. --- Break taken at 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber received a copy of an e-mail sent by Fraser Gilmour addressed to the Registry, a person in the Registry, and I'll read it into the record. First the name of the addressee is mentioned and: "I have just spoken with Mr. Stanisic with the assistance of a language assistant to avoid any problems of misinterpretation. I explained the situation to him and informed him that the Chamber would like to know if he wishes to participate in proceedings via videolink. Mr. Stanisic refused the opportunity." Then it continues: "I left a copy of the following section of the transcript for Mr. Stanisic to read in his own time." And then the section starts with: "The Chamber has considered how to proceed and the Chamber would like the Registrar ..." which we find on today's transcript at 15.58.41 up to 16.00.34, the last words being about the result of this information to be conveyed to the accused. "Regards." That is put on the record. In view of the present situation we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: May I briefly, before the Prosecution starts with its opening, address the Court with a request to the Chamber. We humbly request the Chamber to instruct the Registrar to, if possible, have the first psychiatric report available timely before the 29th of June. Many of the reasons can be adduced for this, but one of the reasons is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops. This is a request which could have been easily addressed at another moment and even informally. Let's focus today on what we're here for now after we have decided whether or not to proceed, and just perhaps for the parties to explain. Everything that can be settled without any negative consequences out of court we should not use court time for that. We are limited in our time, and first of all it goes almost without saying that the Chamber has taken the initiative already that of course we start to have the first report as soon as possible. Also in view of the frequency. But this is not necessarily -- and let me just explain to you, we have -- for informal communications there are three different kinds. The one is purely practical, it can be exchanged without leaving any traces on the record, such as are we moving tomorrow from Courtroom I to Courtroom II, these are matters. If it has some substance, then I'll put it on the record by referring to it in court, as I did, for example, today. And if it's of great importance, then the Chamber will invite the parties to file it. Let's proceed -- the message is clear, Mr. Knoops, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, in view of the fact that Mr. Stanisic has not opted for following the proceedings, this means that we can have the usual court schedules, which means that we have two and a half hours to go. I would say I leave it to you how to split that up and if -- I think it was announced that you would need three hours. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My best estimate, Your Honour, is that the opening would take three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three and a half hours. Then we have one more hour to go tomorrow. I leave it to you where to have the break. We are relatively flexible in view of the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I begin, I will be showing different evidence and other documents on slides. If the Chamber and all parties in the court would so kindly press the e-court button they will be available. I would also ask at this time if the Court Usher would distribute to the Chamber and to the Defence a copy of those slides. It may be that I move past one before you've had a full opportunity to read it. This way you will be able to fully grasp, digest, what's on each of the slides. And I'm providing Defence two copies, one for each accused and one for lead counsel. Your Honour, I'd like to begin my opening with the words of Mr. Jovica Stanisic himself. "We are now entering the decisive phase of the fight to achieve the common goals of all the Serbian lands, more determined and prepared than ever before." These are the words of Mr. Stanisic in a telegram he sent to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska Krajina in Knin in July of 1994. This case will be an exploration of the "common goals of all the Serbian lands" referred to by Mr. Stanisic in his telegram. Specifically, what were those goals, who shared those goals, what were the methods employed to achieve those goals, and most importantly were international crimes committed in pursuit of those goals. Perhaps one of the most shocking pieces of evidence adduced at a trial in this Tribunal is a video containing images of three men and three boys, shot in the back, hands bound tightly with wire. Captured as they fled a fallen Srebrenica, we watch them silently and with resignation walk to the spot where they are murdered one by one. We watch their captors, some mocking the six in their final moments, others demonstrating a demeanour more akin to a routine task, one focusing on capturing the executions on videotape. Here on slide number 3 we see the youngest, Dino Salihovic, moments before he is executed. The world recoiled as the image was played repeatedly on news programmes. The day will come in this trial when we will have to watch their death again, but not today. Today I want to show you a different part of that video. The video taken that day is approximately two hours long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The parts of the video that I want to show you this afternoon, while at first appear less shocking, upon reflection are more disturbing than the killings themselves because they reveal that the perpetrators of these crimes were not rogue paramilitaries, not a band of common criminals; no, the perpetrators of these crimes and the other crimes charged in this indictment were a well-organised and equipped group, part of the special units of the Serbian DB, the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia. Members of a unit that was well trained, well equipped, well paid, they had everything they needed, including a licence to clear land of unwanted peoples, a licence to murder. What is now known about the special units of the Serbian DB has left many Serbs wondering how it was possible that some of the most grievous crimes committed during the war were committed in their name by men paid by the government, men in a unit administered by the State Security Service of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, more specifically by Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic. Your Honours, this case in its simplest terms is an examination of the conduct of two of the people with primary responsibility for organising, training, funding, equipping, and directing members of the special units of the Serbian DB to perpetrate grievous crimes on the territories of Croatia and Bosnia in the name of protecting Serbs and securing for them a land free from Croats and Muslims. Not too long ago a Serb journalist posed the question, in reference to the special units of the Serbian DB: "How did it happen that a group of armed and dangerous men dared to shape the destiny of an entire nation?" Can I draw your attention to the video playing now in slide number 5. Here, in 1997, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic celebrate their work, forgetting the suffering they occasioned, while they pose with current and former members of their special units. The proud founders of that group of armed and dangerous men that so dared to shape the destiny of an entire nation. The tensions that fuelled the break-up of Yugoslavia and the terrible inter-ethnic violence that spared no one are still the subject of scholarly and popular debate, a debate that lies outside the task that the Trial Chamber begins today. The Trial Chamber is not called upon to adjudicate these issues, and I will spend little time on them here. The focus of this trial is upon Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic and the role they played in the commission of crimes in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The role they played in a plan to use violence to forge fundamental demographic changes on the territories of the former Yugoslavia. It is only right that we begin this task by spending a few moments to consider who these two men were at the outset, what were the legal -- what were the legal duties and what were the boundaries of their authority. Both Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic were employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia. I will refer to this ministry throughout this opening by its Serbian acronym, MUP or M-U-P. The Serbian MUP's mandate is articulated in the Serbian Law on Ministries which is reproduced here in relevant part on slide number 7. Its legal authority is similar to other interior ministries in other developed, democratic societies. In essence, it was responsible for the protection of citizens and residents of the country and the regulation of borders, passports, and identity documents. In short, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Serbian MUP, was responsible for the safety and security of persons inside the Republic of Serbia. One of the administrative divisions of the MUP was the State Security Service, the part of the MUP headed by Jovica Stanisic. This section, too, was more commonly known by its Serbian acronym, the DB. Slide number 8 shows Article 3 of the DB's rules, the article which defines its mandate as one of collecting information, data, and knowledge. Information of general and counter-intelligence, information concerning extremism and terrorism. And while it also included the collection of information about "forms of threats to the national and cultural historical identity of Serbs who live outside of the Republic" of Serbia, it clearly sets the legal boundaries of what Mr. Stanisic's organisation was entitled to do: Collect information. Let me now speak directly about Mr. Stanisic and his place in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Slide 9 contains a brief summary of his professional appointments. Jovica Stanisic would join the MUP in 1975. His first position there would be in the State Security Service, the DB. Although throughout 1991 Mr. Stanisic was nominally the deputy head of the DB, the evidence in this case will show that during this period the de facto head of that -- he was also the de facto of that organisation. On the 31st of December, 1991, with Slobodan Milosevic's intervention, he assumed the position of head or chief of the DB. As you can see from slide 10, Mr. Stanisic had the responsibility of implementing the mandate of the Serbian DB. I would also like to point out the penultimate paragraph "organises the execution of tasks and affairs within the competence of the Division in conditions of emergency" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, it's common experience that when you're reading that you speed up. The French interpreters were at least a couple of lines behind, so I'd like to invite you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you. I would also like to point out the penultimate paragraph "organises the execution of tasks and affairs within the competence of the Division in conditions of emergency, imminent threat of war, and war." Although there was conflict in Croatia and Bosnia from 1991 until 1995, Serbia itself never ever declared a state of emergency or imminent threat of war, and thus this paragraph never became effective during the period of this indictment. Let me now turn your attention to the career of Franko Simatovic. Slide number 11 is a brief summary of his resume. He would join the DB three years after Stanisic in 1978. He worked in the section responsible for gathering intelligence. As you can see from this description of Mr. Simatovic's job on slide 12, he was primarily charged with implementing projects to gather intelligence, data, and information about threats to Serbia. While the mandate extends to collecting information about perceived threats to ethnic Serbs living outside of Serbia, it does not provide for any forcible intervention outside the country. The internal laws of Serbia are laws similar to other modern states, laws designed to circumscribe the activities of a governmental organ with precision and maintain a balance of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I have to repeat my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They are there to ensure that the authority of the state is not misused. While ideologically Stanisic and Simatovic identified with Slobodan Milosevic and his goals for the Serb people, the laws of Serbia prevented them from deploying their personnel as a fighting force outside Serbia's borders, in Croatia and Bosnia. When Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina declared independence, the presence of the Yugoslav Army there was no longer legitimate. It became necessary for Milosevic to create a paramilitary force that could be deployed covertly outside Serbia and outside Serbia's laws, a paramilitary force that could be used in combat as well as in the commission of the crimes necessary to implement Milosevic's goal of creating ethnically pure areas in Croatia and Bosnia. The State Security Service, already engaged in covert information gathering, was a logical place to create such a special unit. If the state is going to engage in criminal conduct, it will use its secret services to engage in that conduct --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I raise with hesitance, but is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it the personal opinion of the Prosecution we hear or is it an opening statement without argument? It is improper in an opening statement to argue a case on the basis of personal opinions and views of the Prosecution. So I object if this is an opening statement whereby the Prosecution presents its personal view on the relationship between the accused and Mr. Milosevic and the DB and their goals or their policies. An opening statement is meant to present what the evidence will be presented by the Prosecution; it's not meant to be an argument. It's not meant to be -- provide the personal opinion of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, did you intend to do anything else than to tell the Court what you will establish by presenting your evidence or do you go beyond that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The two things that I believe I'm charged with here is letting the Chamber as well as the accused themselves know what the theory of the Prosecution case is as well as give an overview of the evidence, and those are the two things that I intend to do, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is what you intend to prove and what is underlying your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, I do not see that there's anything wrong with that, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, maybe then the Prosecutor should for the Defence's sake differentiate between what the evidence is going to say and what the view is of the Prosecution's theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the two are intrinsically intertwined I would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would note that all of the evidence is clearly marked, as you will in the slides, with the 65 ter number so the Defence will be very -- it will be very clear to the Defence what is specifically evidence and what is the theory of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. At the same time, you're invited to keep in the back of your mind what apparently is of concern for Mr. Knoops. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, throughout the course of this opening the Prosecution will introduce you to some of the people who are central to this case. Each of the people we speak about in this way is a core member of a joint criminal enterprise with Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic or were prominent members of the special units of the Serbian DB. One of the people the Chamber will hear a great deal about is Slobodan Milosevic. It has always been the position of the Office of the Prosecutor that he was the central driving force behind this joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution will tender evidence in this trial showing the close working relationship that the two accused had with Mr. Milosevic. In October 1998 when Stanisic was dismissed by Milosevic he gave a public statement. In that statement shown here on slide 13, Stanisic states that he executed his duties within his constitutional and legal powers. The Chamber's adjudication of this indictment will test the accuracy of this statement. He also made clear that he had aligned himself with President Milosevic in the early 1990s. A careful examination of Serbia's law at that time will make clear that such an arrangement circumvented the legally defined chain of authority. Mihalj Kertes, like Jovica Stanisic, was born in a place in Serbia called Backa Palanka. He was the head of the security department in one of Serbia's largest banks, the Dafinement Bank, and secured the financing for Jovica Stanisic to create the special units of the Serbian DB. I would like to play an intercept for you, the translation is on slide 14, and we hear Kertes and Karadzic talk about the problems Mr. Stanisic is having with his lawful superior, a person by the name of Mr. Janackovic, suggesting that his trust in Mr. Janackovic was misplaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we read it in English. The audio is just in B/C/S. We have no French translation of it, so we have an incomplete record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had provided all the booths with the text, but I see now that I omit to have provided them a copy with the slides. I will do that as soon as I can so that they have the text that they can work from as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because this is just for informing the parties. If any audio or if any video is played with sound, then I expect the parties to provide in advance a transcript to the booths so that the booths can translate into the relevant language the text spoken. Now, sometimes the speed of speech is such that it may be difficult to translate and then the booths are invited that one of the interpreters follows on the text whether that reflects the words spoken and that the, if I could say the teammate would then translate on the basis of the transcript, which finally results in a complete record where we have the original and the relevant translations. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask if the usher could provide to the French booth a copy of the slides in the event that they're unable to read it from the screen. An electronic copy is also being sent as we speak. Your Honour, we heard in this intercept Kertes saying that Milosevic had given Mr. -- him and Mr. Stanisic carte blanche. I would like to show you a clip from a video we refer to several times in this opening. The video was taken during an awards ceremony at the Radoslav Kostic Training Centre in Kula, Serbia, in May of 1997. Many of the people who were behind the formation of the special units of the Serbian DB and supported its activities in Croatia and Bosnia attended. During this clip, Jovica Stanisic is giving Milosevic a tour of the facility and handing out awards to those who played a prominent role in the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we play it, can I just verify with the booths whether the system is now in place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note in the English booth the system is not in place. We don't have the text and the screen keeps flashing on and off, e-court screen, so we can't read it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME

I'm not sure what has happened today. I have another copy, Your Honour, that we can provide the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we wait until it has been provided to the English booth and then everyone's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher is busy copying for all the booths so we have to take our time, otherwise we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I might. If it's of assistance, I provided six copies for the Chamber. If all of those copies are not in use, if -- well, I think --

utterances.text: My copy is available at this very moment for the English booth and I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have the text. Thank you very much.

utterances.text: We'll replace those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could someone give it to the -- perhaps if everyone stays in this courtroom, they'll never be received by the booths. I'm not criticising anyone and the last person I would expect to do it would be our Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being done --

utterances.text: Mr. Groome, under those circumstances, I expect one of your team members to immediately receive that and give it to the booths instead of making the Registrar leave the courtroom and do the job.
